title: The Creed's shape (CCC 190)
hook: three parts: Father and creation, Son and redemption, Spirit and sanctification

segments.voice: Yesterday, I believe, we believe: faith that's personal and never solitary. Your line was no one believes alone. Who did you thank? Today, the shape of what's believed. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

Break a seal in two. Keep one half, and give the other to a friend who's leaving for somewhere far away. Years later, a stranger knocks at your door and holds out a jagged piece. You take out yours and put the edges together. If they fit, you know who sent this person. In Greek, a token like that was called a symbolon. The Catechism says it's an old name for the Creed: a sign by which believers recognize each other. Today we look at the shape of that piece: the Creed's shape.
screen: `A SEAL BROKEN IN TWO.` → `DO THE EDGES FIT?` → `THE CREED AS A SYMBOLON.`

segments.voice: Where does the Creed's shape come from? The Catechism points to baptism. Jesus sends the apostles out, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Because the faith is first professed at baptism, the Catechism says, the Creed is built around those same three names. So it falls into three parts. The first speaks of the Father and the work of creation. The second, of the Son and the mystery of redemption. The third, of the Holy Spirit, the source of our sanctification, the making holy of people. Father, creation. Son, redemption. Spirit, sanctification. Three movements, and the Catechism borrows that division from an older catechism, the Roman Catechism, which followed the same plan. A few things are worth noticing. First, it's a story as much as a list. The Creed moves: from the making of all things, to the rescue of what went wrong, to the slow work of making people holy, ending with eternal life. Second, three parts don't mean three gods. The Creed confesses one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and Catholic teaching holds that all three are at work in every part; the division says which work is chiefly spoken of where. Third, the shape is useful. If you ever lose your place in the Creed, the turns are easy to find: one where it comes to Jesus Christ, the Son, and one where it comes to the Holy Spirit. That's the carry: three movements. One God, making, saving and making holy.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON, SPIRIT.` · `FATHER: CREATION.` · `SON: REDEMPTION. SPIRIT: SANCTIFICATION.` · `ONE GOD, NOT THREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark the three parts in the Creed. If you have it in a missal, a prayer book or on your phone, read it through slowly, and mark the two places where it turns: to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. If you don't have it in front of you, walk through the three movements instead. Settle, and breathe. On one breath, think of something made: the world, your own body. On the next, something mended. On the next, something growing better, slowly. Go around the three, as many times as the bell allows. If you pray, you can name each movement to God. The bell holds the time.
The Creed's shape. Three parts: the Father and creation, the Son and redemption, the Spirit and sanctification, all one God. Today's word.
Your line: three movements. Today, notice one thing being made, one thing being mended, and one thing slowly getting better, and name all three. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics profess the Creed at Sunday Mass and at baptism, and the Catechism's first part is laid out in the Creed's order, beginning with the Father and creation, then the Son, then the Holy Spirit.

fork.setup: a stranger arrives with half of a broken seal and says a friend sent them. how do you check?
fork.reveal: if the edges fit, the bearer is who they claim. the Catechism says the Creed's old Greek name, symbolon, comes from a token like that: a sign of recognition between believers.

original.note: Greek: half of a broken object, a token of recognition. The Catechism gives it as an old name for the Creed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Creed is a list of beliefs in no special order.
what it means: a creed shaped in three parts, Father and creation, Son and redemption, Spirit and sanctification.
what a scholar hears: CCC 190, following the Roman Catechism, and CCC 188's symbolon, a broken token fitted back together.
recall: one of the four Gospel writers, like John

notes: Catechism paraphrased (copyright): symbolon as half of a broken object, a token of recognition, a sign between believers (CCC 188); the Creed as the baptismal profession structured by the three Persons (CCC 189); the three parts, from the Roman Catechism (CCC 190). Confirm.

'Catholic teaching holds that all three are at work in every part; the division says which work is chiefly spoken of where': summary of the doctrine of the inseparable operations and appropriations (cf. CCC 258), outside the day's range. Keeper may trim.
Hook's seal story elaborates CCC 188's example (a seal presented as a token of recognition); the 'friend leaving' scene is illustrative.
'the life of the world to come' echoes the Creed's closing phrase without quotation marks; confirm.
Practice: 'and in his Son, and in the Holy Spirit' as the turns in the Creed; wording differs slightly between the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds.
Original: σύμβολον; confirm accent and pronunciation.

Editor: the Creed's turns were given as 'and in his Son', words neither creed uses; now described, not quoted. Ending changed to 'eternal life' to fit both creeds. Myth item 'arranged by century' replaced, since day 1062's fork used the same 'by century' foil.
